newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Tension mounts in Karachi ahead of elections.
newsitem.headline: Tension mounts in Karachi ahead of elections.

text.p: Tension is building in violence-prone Karachi, Pakistan's commercial capital, as nationwide elections approach, despite a singularly lacklustre campaign.

At least three people have died in the past week in clashes between supporters of the ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM), which is expected to win most of the seats in Karachi, and the splinter MQM Haqiqi faction.
Each side accuses the other of unprovoked aggression and of not allowing it to campaign in the other's areas of influence.
"Twice and in two different localities we were forced out of our election offices, which were later burnt," said MQM coordination committee chief Ishtiaq Azhar.
Afaq Ahmad, head of the MQM Haqiqi, threatened to boycott the February 3 elections and to call a protest strike on polling day unless his candidates were given freedom to campaign.
"We will shut down the urban areas of Sindh if the government does not ensure a free and impartial election and allow us to contest freely," Ahmad said last week.

Karachi is the capital of Sindh province and the majority of its estimated 12 million population are mohajirs, Urdu-speaking Moslems who left Hindu-majority India when Pakistan was formed in 1947 at the end of the British Raj.
Mohajirs have often been at odds with Karachi's other ethnic groups, including Sindhis, Pashtuns, Punjabis and Baluchis.

Thousands of people have been killed in years of often ferocious violence in Karachi as the MQM campaigned against what it said was discrimination against mohajirs, though the unrest has cooled considerably in recent months.

In the run-up to the polls, the MQM has been the most active party, holding rallies around the city. Campaigning by other parties has been low-key, with few people attending public meetings, partly because of fear of inter-MQM clashes.
Benazir Bhutto, dismissed as prime minister by President Farooq Leghari in November on disputed corruption charges, has attracted only thin crowds at her appearances in Karachi.
Imran Khan, cricket star turned politician, has not been seen, although he is contesting two Karachi constituencies.
Nazim Haji, the Sindh provincial chief organiser of Khan's Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement), said voters and candidates were still unsure if elections would actually take place.
The Supreme Court is expected to rule this week on Bhutto's petition challenging her dismissal and seeking reinstatement.
"Some new restrictions like the ban on flags, banners and wall-chalking and a smaller permitted campaign budget have also kept the campaign quite dull," Haji said.

He said his party was working hard to make its presence felt but agreed it would be difficult to erode support for the MQM, which boycotted the last polls in 1993 after winning 11 of Karachi's 13 National Assembly seats three years earlier.

"We think a lot of the Punjabi and Pashtun vote will go for Imran," he said in a constituency where Imran, an ethnic Pashtun who lives in Punjab, faces Naseerullah Babar, Bhutto's former interior minister and scourge of the MQM.
Contesting the same seat are candidates for the MQM and the Pakistan Muslim Leaque led by Nawaz Sharif, who is widely expected to lead his party to nationwide victory at the polls.
The only Karachi seat Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party is seen as sure to win is Lyari, a slum constituency dominated by ethnic Baluchis, where it has won in every election since 1970.
